newsitem.title: UK: UK food, farming industry form strategy group.
newsitem.headline: UK food, farming industry form strategy group.

text.p: Britain's farming and food industry launched an influential advisory body on Tuesday called the Food Project in an effort to make the industry more competitive and forestall another beef crisis.

Chairman of the Project's strategy group Peter Barr told a news conference, "I do not think it will eliminate the risk of another crisis but it will make us very much more aware of problems facing the industry."

The food project will act as an advisory body to the industry, putting forward initiatives and as an action group to tackle particular sector issues like beef, poultry and horticulture and dairy. The project has the support of the government's Ministry of Agriculture (MAFF) and will be run under the auspices of the Institute of Grocery Distribution.

Britain's food industry is still suffering damage caused by the former Conservative government's admission in March 1996 that mad cow disease, or bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), could be linked to a fatal human illness, Creutzfeld-Jakob-Disease(CJD).

A crippling ban on the export of British beef into Europe has been in place since March 1996. Consumer confidence at home has also yet to recover while farmers are receiving just 85-90 pence a kilo down from 125 pence before the crisis.
The beef crisis has made Britain's food industry more aware of consumers needs and the importance of looking at the food chain as a whole, said Barr.
"We will aim to work with industry from plough to the plate," said Barr.

Consumers now want to know more about the methods of food production and other information enabling them to trace the entire supply chain. The food chain is now largely driven by consumers whereas it used to be supply driven, he said.

The single most important aim of the Project is "to ensure that this country remains competitive," said Barr. It will encourage producers, retailers and manufacturers to look overseas "to benchmark against the best," he said.
Britain's farmers face increased competition from overseas as trade barriers come down and more technology is introduced, said Tony Pexton, vice president of the National Farmers Union.
Retailers and manufacturers now look round the world for the best suppliers and farmers can no longer take their route to the consumer for granted.

Britain has 130,000 working farms, a number which industry analysts acknowledge is not sustainable given that the current level of subsidy from the European Commission is likely to fall especially if the European Union expands eastward.

Members of the food project strategy group include Peter Barr, also chairman of Hazelwood Foods, and representative from Safeway, Nestle (UK) Ltd, J. Sainsbury, Asda, Whitbread, Marks & Spencer, Tesco, MAFF and the National Farmers Union.
